---
title: "Working with dates"
---

One of the most frustrating things in data is working with dates. Everyone has a different opinion on how to record them, and every software package on the planet has to sort it out. Dealing with it can be a little ... confusing. And every dataset has something new to throw at you. So consider this an introduction.

First, there's the right way to display dates in data. Most of the rest of the world knows how to do this, but Americans aren't taught it. The correct way to display dates is the following format: YYYY-MM-DD, or 2022-09-15. Any date that looks different should be converted into that format when you're using R.

Luckily, this problem is so common that the Tidyverse has an entire library for dealing with it: [lubridate](https://lubridate.tidyverse.org/).

We're going to do this two ways. First I'm going to show you how to use base R to solve a tricky problem. And then we'll use a library called `lubridate` to solve a more common and less tricky problem. And then we'll use a new library to solve most of the common problems before they start. If it's not already installed, just run `install.packages('lubridate')`

## Making dates dates again

First, we'll import `tidyverse` like we always do and our newly-installed lubridate.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
```
:::


Let's start with a dataset of 2025 payments from drug and medical device companies to Maryland health care providers, from the federal Open Payments database. It's a big file -- more than 300,000 payments -- so it's been compressed; `read_csv()` can read compressed .gz files directly:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
md_payments <- read_csv("data/md_open_payments_2025.csv.gz")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```

i Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
head(md_payments)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 6 x 15
   record_id date_of_payment recipient_type        recipient_name recipient_city
       <dbl> <chr>           <chr>                 <chr>          <chr>         
1 1163236989 01/11/2025      Non-Physician Practi~ Travis Baird   Glen burnie   
2 1163253642 03/26/2025      Physician             ALTA WOLDE     ROCKVILLE     
3 1172026065 03/26/2025      Non-Physician Practi~ TIMOTHY LEDER~ Abingdon

6 1173623966 10/15/2025      Physician             BOAZ ROSEN     ANNAPOLIS     
# i 10 more variables: recipient_zip <dbl>, specialty <chr>, company <chr>,

#   product_name <chr>
```


:::
:::


Take a look at the second column, date_of_payment. It *looks* like a date, but see the `<chr` right below the column name? That means R thinks it's actually a character column. What we need to do is make it into an actual date column, which lubridate is very good at doing. It has a variety of functions that match the format of the data you have. In this case, the current format is `m/d/y`, and the lubridate function is called `mdy` that we can use with mutate:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
md_payments <- md_payments |> mutate(date_of_payment=mdy(date_of_payment))

head(md_payments)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 6 x 15
   record_id date_of_payment recipient_type        recipient_name recipient_city
       <dbl> <date>          <chr>                 <chr>          <chr>

2 1163253642 2025-03-26      Physician             ALTA WOLDE     ROCKVILLE     
3 1172026065 2025-03-26      Non-Physician Practi~ TIMOTHY LEDER~ Abingdon      
4 1172031309 2025-08-20      Non-Physician Practi~ MARTHA REILLEY Baltimore     
5 1172032666 2025-10-27      Non-Physician Practi~ SHERYL DEGUZM~ Clinton       
6 1173623966 2025-10-15      Physician             BOAZ ROSEN     ANNAPOLIS     
# i 10 more variables: recipient_zip <dbl>, specialty <chr>, company <chr>,

#   nature_of_payment <chr>, form_of_payment <chr>, product_type <chr>,
#   product_name <chr>
```


:::
:::


Now look at the date_of_payment column: R says it's a date column and it looks like we want it to: YYYY-MM-DD. Accept no substitutes.

Lubridate has functions for basically any type of character date format: mdy, ymd, even datetimes like ymd_hms.

That's less code and less weirdness, so that's good.

But to get clean data, I've installed a library and created a new field so I can now start to work with my dates. That seems like a lot, but don't think your data will always be perfect and you won't have to do these things.

Still, there's got to be a better way. And there is.

Fortunately, `readr` anticipates some date formatting and can automatically handle many of these issues (indeed it uses lubridate under the hood). When you are importing a CSV file, be sure to use `read_csv`, not `read.csv`.

But you're not done with lubridate yet. It has some interesting pieces parts we'll use elsewhere.

For example, in spreadsheets you can extract portions of dates - a month, day or year - with formulas. You can do the same in R with lubridate. Let's say we wanted to add up the total amount paid in each month in our payments data.

We could use formatting to create a Month field but that would group all the Aprils ever together. We could create a year and a month together, but that would give us an invalid date object and that would create problems later. Lubridate has something called a floor date that we can use.

So to follow along here, we're going to use mutate to create a month field, group by to lump them together, summarize to count them up and arrange to order them. We're just chaining things together.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
md_payments |>
  mutate(month = floor_date(date_of_payment, "month")) |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarise(total_amount = sum(amount)) |>
  arrange(desc(total_amount))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 12 x 2
   month      total_amount
   <date>            <dbl>
 1 2025-07-01    24251014.
 2 2025-08-01     7053349.
 3 2025-05-01     6385924.
 4 2025-12-01     5945861.
 5 2025-02-01     5836927.
 6 2025-11-01     5461856.
 7 2025-10-01     4920646.
 8 2025-04-01     4686714.
 9 2025-06-01     4392660.
10 2025-03-01     4054216.
11 2025-09-01     3837292.
12 2025-01-01     3508952.
```


:::
:::


So the month of July 2025 had the most money paid by far in this data -- more than three times as much as any other month. Is that a pattern, like companies paying for a big medical conference? Sort the payments by amount and you'll see that it's mostly a single payment: more than \$20 million from a medical device company to one Maryland physician, listed as an "Acquisition" -- the kind of payment a company makes when it buys a business or technology a doctor helped create. One huge payment can make a monthly total misleading, which is why you should always look at the individual records behind a big number.
